newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FEATURE - Mergers seen in Philippine telecom.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Mergers seen in Philippine telecom.

text.p: Philippine telecommunications companies threatened with fraud, stiff competition and worry about rates will have to forge alliances and mergers to survive.

"We foresee consolidation and mergers because the sector is too crowded. To better serve economies of scale, they have to merge and we now see the emergence of these tie-ups especially in installing landlines," said Saturnino Mejia, research head at Guoco Securities.
"The prospects of mergers are good as we see players wanting bigger territories and resources," National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) head Simeon Kintanar told Reuters.
At present, the Philippines has 11 international gateway facility (IGF) operators, 12 paging operators, five cellular phone companies and 11 local exchange operators.

The NTC has required IGF operators to install 300,000 landlines in exchange for their permits while cellular phone operators are mandated to put up 400,000 lines, all in a period of three years or by early next year.
MERGERS SEEN AS BEST WAY TO RAISE CASH
"Mergers are a very real possibility as raising cash for these companies will be tough. Definitely, the big ones will reign," said Russell Ong, analyst at Anscor-Hagedorn Securities Inc.
Pilipino Telephone Corp (Piltel) started the ball rolling last February when it signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) and alliance with Major Telecommunications Inc (MajorTel).
MajorTel is a subsidiary of IGF operator Philippine Global Communications (Philcom) and under the MOU it will, with Piltel, set up telecommunications facilities in the southern region of Mindanao.
Another cellular phone firm, Smart Communications Co Inc, a subsidiary of Metro Pacific Corp, also bought into IGF operator Eastern Telecommunications Philippines Inc last year.

"The NTC has been saying that the service areas of those who will not meet their roll-out programmes will have to be given as a reward to those who are complying and if that is true, some companies who are delayed may be forced to merge," said Roberto Cano, investment analyst at BPI Capital Corp.
"The name of the game is to generate and improve cash flow and unfortunately the cellular phone firms are experiencing fraud," said one analyst from a big foreign brokerage firm.
MOBILE PHONE COMPANIES HIT BY FRAUD
Cellular phone companies were hit with a major problem of fraud, cloning and bad subscriber debts in 1996.
"Everyone emphasized marketing so the companies were caught off guard and experienced fraud," said Cano.

Piltel, the cellular firm with the biggest subscriber base, has set aside 886.352 million pesos ($33.7 million) in 1996 from 80.93 million in 1995 for doubtful accounts. The company reported on March 5 a net income of 710.468 million pesos, down from an original net forecast of 1.16 billion pesos.
A day after the results were announced, Piltel's stock fell in intra-day trading to a year-low of 14.25 pesos.

Globe Telecom GMCR Inc, a joint venture of Ayala Corp and Singapore Telecom also suffered subscription fraud and set aside 725.4 million pesos in 1996 as provision for bad debts. The company suffered a net loss of 750.9 million pesos last year from 155.4 million a year earlier.

"Telecom stocks have good fundamental values but they have to prove that they can overcome these problems, that they are really clone-proof," said Helen Alvarez, research director at All Asia Securities.
Telecom companies are also plagued by worries about a reduction in accounting rates or the cost of international calls, which will mean lower revenues for them.
The United States Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has said it is planning to reduce accounting rates from $1.00 to $0.38 a minute.
DESPITE PROBLEMS, TELECOMS STILL A GOOD INVESTMENT
Despite the problems facing the telecommunications companies, analysts said they were still good investments.
"The cellular phone industry is not dead but better management systems are needed," said UBS Securities (East Asia) Ltd in an industry outlook report.
"The sector will continue to be attractive given the companies' telephone density and economic growth. There is demand," said BPI's Cano.
As of end-1996, the NTC said the country's total telephone density is 4.09 per 100 persons from 2.1 in 1995.
By year-end, Kintanar said, he expects the number to double.
"Assuming a good scenario that we can contain subscription and cloning problems, we can say profits of the sector will grow by 30 to 40 percent this year," said Guoco's Mejia.
Local exchange operators would register earnings growth of 20 to 25 percent, he added.

Although the growth of cellular phone companies may be limited by fraud problems, All Asia's Alvarez said these firms are likely to solve the problem if all their promised anti-fraud measures are put in place.
"We maintain our bullishness on the sector but advise a cautious stance on cellular stocks," said Alvarez.
($ = 26.34 Philippine Pesos)
